summary: Common buckthorn, also called European buckthorn, is a large shrub or small tree up to about 20 feet tall. It forms thick hedges whose long branches crowd out and shade out native shrubs and wildflowers and stop native plants from regrowing. Its leaf litter is high in nitrogen and changes the soil in ways that help buckthorn keep growing. It also hosts a fungus that damages oat crops and an aphid that harms soybeans.
history: Common buckthorn is native to most of Europe and western Asia. It was brought to North America in the 1800s as an ornamental shrub and windbreak, but did not spread widely until the early 1900s.
seasons: Small yellowish-green flowers bloom in late spring (May and June) while the leaves are coming out. Its dark purple to black berries ripen in August and September and can stay on the plant all winter. Birds and other wildlife spread the seeds, which can stay alive in the soil for up to five years.

handling.text: Its branches end in a short, sharp thorn. Plants can be removed by hand or with machines depending on their size, and repeated mowing and cutting weakens them. Because seeds last in the soil for five years, cleared areas need follow-up. In New York City parks like Kissena, cutting, killing or removing plants without permission from NYC Parks is against park rules, so report it instead.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks like Kissena Park, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
